entities.summary:
Clitomachus of Thebes (died 260 BCE) was an ancient Greek pankratiast, boxer, and wrestler, active in the early 3rd century BCE, who achieved legendary status for his extraordinary athletic prowess and unique training methods. He represents the pinnacle of combat sports during the Hellenistic period, an era when individual athletic achievement was deeply intertwined with civic pride and interstate rivalry within the Greek world. His career spanned a time marked by the Diadochi wars and the consolidation of Hellenistic kingdoms, where athletic festivals like the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian Games offered a rare arena for peaceful competition and cultural expression. His fame was such that he was considered among the greatest combat athletes of all time, alongside figures like Milo of Croton.

Clitomachus achieved the rare distinction of winning championships at all four Panhellenic Games—the Olympics, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian—a feat known as a *periodonikes*. His most celebrated achievement occurred in 264 BCE at the 130th Olympic Games, where he won the pankration title. He was also a victor in boxing and wrestling, demonstrating a versatility that was highly unusual even for elite athletes of his time. Ancient sources, notably Pausanias and Philostratus, recount his rigorous training regimen, which included strict dietary control and a disciplined lifestyle. He famously refused to eat bread during his training, a testament to his dedication.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Clitomachus's achievement of *periodonikes* status and his legendary dedication set a high bar for athletic excellence in the ancient world, impacting the cultural ideal of *arete* for centuries. His fame brought significant prestige to Thebes during a politically tumultuous era, reinforcing the role of athletics in civic identity.
